reference_title: Design and Construction of Driven Pile Foundations

sections.title: Introduction
sections.summary: Systematic selection of foundation type based on superstructure requirements, subsurface conditions, and cost. Foundation types: shallow (spread footings, mats) and deep (driven piles, micropiles, drilled shafts, CFA piles). Table 3-1 lists FHWA reference manuals for each foundation type.
sections.body: (p. 45) A foundation is the interfacing element between the superstructure, substructure, and the underlying geomaterial. The loads transmitted by the foundation must not cause shear failure or damaging deformations of the superstructure. It is essential to systematically consider various foundation types and to select the most appropriate alternative based on the superstructure requirements, the subsurface conditions, and foundation cost. Foundation types include shallow foundations (spread footings, mat foundations with or without ground improvement) and deep foundations (driven piles, micropiles, drilled shafts, CFA piles). Table 3-1 lists the FHWA guidance for other foundation solutions: spread footings (GEC-6, FHWA-SA-02-054, Kimmerling 2002), ground improvement (FHWA-NHI-06-019/020, Elias et al. 2006), micropiles (FHWA-NHI-05-039, Sabatini et al. 2005), drilled shafts (GEC-10, FHWA NHI-10-016, Brown et al. 2010) and CFA piles (GEC-8, FHWA-HIF-07-03, Brown et al. 2007).
key_points: Foundation interfaces superstructure/substructure with underlying geomaterial
Must not cause shear failure or damaging deformations
Systematic evaluation of foundation types required
Selection based on superstructure requirements, subsurface conditions, and cost
FHWA provides separate manuals for other foundation types (Table 3-1: GEC-6, ground improvement, micropiles, GEC-10, GEC-8)

sections.title: Foundation Design Approach
sections.summary: Six-step foundation selection process: (1) define loads and constraints, (2) evaluate subsurface data, (3) prepare final profile, (4) identify feasible alternatives, (5) prepare cost estimates using foundation support cost concept, (6) select most economical option. If alternatives are within 15% cost, include alternates in contract documents.
sections.body: (pp. 46-47) A six-step approach is recommended to find the most appropriate foundation alternative. (1) Determine the foundation loads, structure layout, limits on total and differential settlement and lateral deformation, lateral loads, scour, seismic and other extreme event loading, and special requirements such as construction phasing and time constraints. (2) Evaluate the subsurface exploration and laboratory data, and if insufficient perform a second exploration, laboratory or in-situ testing program. (3) Prepare a final subsurface profile and critical cross sections, identify layers suitable or unsuitable for spread footings, piles or drilled shafts, and consider whether ground improvement could make unsuitable layers suitable. (4) Determine the most feasible alternatives, shallow (spread footings without ground improvement, mats) and deep (driven piles, candidate pile types, viable sections, drilled shafts, micropiles, CFA piles); proprietary deep foundation systems should not be excluded. (5) Prepare cost estimates using the foundation support cost of Section 3.4.1, including temporary and permanent substructure costs (sheeting or cofferdams, tremie seal, pile cap size), environmental and construction limitations (noise, vibration, low overhead, access) and mitigation (noise shrouds, predrilling, bubble nets). (6) Select the most appropriate alternative, generally the lowest foundation support cost, considering local construction ability and material and equipment availability. For major projects with feasible alternatives within 15 percent of each other in estimated cost, alternate designs should be considered for the contract documents, so construction demand and material pricing decide.
key_points: Step 1: Determine foundation loads, structure layout, settlement/deformation limits, scour, seismic, and construction constraints
Step 2: Evaluate subsurface exploration and laboratory testing data; perform additional testing if insufficient
Step 3: Prepare final subsurface profile and critical cross sections; identify suitable and unsuitable bearing layers
Step 4: Determine feasible foundation alternatives including shallow foundations, driven piles, drilled shafts, micropiles, and CFA piles
Proprietary deep foundation systems should not be excluded; they may be the most economical in a given condition
Step 5: Prepare cost estimates using foundation support cost concept (Section 3.4.1) including all substructure and construction control costs
Step 6: Select the most economical alternative considering local construction capability and material availability
If feasible alternatives are within 15% cost of each other, include alternate designs in contract documents
Foundation options include spread footings, mat foundations, driven piles, candidate pile types, viable pile sections, drilled shafts, micropiles, and CFA piles
sections.applicability: Systematic foundation selection process for all transportation structure projects.

sections.title: Foundation Alternatives
sections.summary: Driven piles are the most commonly used deep foundation for transportation projects. Table 3-2 compares spread footings, mats, driven piles, drilled shafts, micropiles (diameter < 12 in.), and CFA piles — listing applicable and non-suitable soil conditions for each. Deep foundations should not be used indiscriminately where installation is difficult or costly.
sections.body: (pp. 47-48) Both shallow and deep foundations should be considered to find the preferred alternative. Table 3-2 (modified from Bowles 1977) summarizes the use, applicable soil conditions and non-suitable or difficult soil conditions of spread and wall footings, mat foundations, driven piles, drilled shafts, micropiles and CFA piles. Driven pile foundations suit poor surface and near surface soils with suitable geomaterials 15 to 300 ft below ground and are difficult with a shallow hard stratum, where vibrations or heave would harm adjacent facilities, and in boulder fields; drilled shafts suit suitable geomaterial 25 to 300 ft below ground and are difficult in caving formations, artesian conditions, boulder fields and contaminated soil; micropiles suit any soil, rock or fill including rubble, boulders and karst, with buckling concerns in liquefiable soils and low lateral resistance.
key_points: Consider both shallow and deep foundations (Table 3-2, modified from Bowles 1977)
Spread footings: any condition with adequate bearing; not on soils subject to excessive scour or liquefaction
Mat foundations: very heavy column loads; reduce differential and total settlement
Driven piles: suitable layers 15 to 300 ft deep; difficult with shallow hard stratum, vibration or heave sensitive neighbors, boulder fields
Drilled shafts: suitable layers 25 to 300 ft deep; difficult in caving formations, artesian conditions, boulders, contaminated soil
Micropiles: any soil, rock or fill incl. rubble, boulders, karst; buckling in liquefiable soils, low lateral resistance, offshore
CFA piles: difficult in very soft soils, loose saturated sands, karst, flowing water, highly variable conditions, long piles
tables: Table 3-2: Foundation Types and Typical Uses (Modified from Bowles 1977) (p. 48) - columns: Foundation Type; Use; Applicable Soil Conditions; Non-suitable or Difficult Soil Conditions (each cell below is named by its column). Spread footing, wall footings. Use: Individual columns, walls, bridge piers. Applicable Soil Conditions: Any conditions where bearing capacity is adequate for applied load. May use on single stratum; firm layer over soft layer, or weaker layer over firm layer. Check immediate, differential and consolidation settlements. Non-suitable or Difficult Soil Conditions: Any conditions where foundations are supported on soils subject to excessive scour or liquefaction. | Mat foundation. Use: Same as spread and wall footings. Very heavy column loads. Usually reduces differential settlements and total settlements. Applicable Soil Conditions: Generally soil bearing value is less than for spread footings. Over one-half area of structure covered by individual footings. Check settlements. Non-suitable or Difficult Soil Conditions: Same as footings. | Driven pile foundations. Use: In groups to transfer heavy column and bridge loads to suitable soil and rock layers. Also to resist uplift and/or lateral loads. Applicable Soil Conditions: Poor surface and near surface soils. Geomaterials suitable for load support 15 to 300 feet below ground surface. Check settlement and lateral deformation of pile groups. Non-suitable or Difficult Soil Conditions: Shallow depth to hard stratum. Sites where pile driving vibrations or heave would adversely impact adjacent facilities. Boulder fields. | Drilled shafts. Use: In groups to transfer heavy column loads. Monoshafts and small groups sometimes used. Cap sometimes eliminated by using drilled shafts as column extensions. Applicable Soil Conditions: Poor surface and near surface soils. Geomaterial suitable for load support located 25 to 300 feet below ground surface. Non-suitable or Difficult Soil Conditions: Caving formations difficult to stabilize. Artesian conditions. Boulder fields. Contaminated soil. Areas with concrete delivery or concrete placement logistic problems. | Micropiles. Use: Often used for seismic retrofitting, underpinning, very difficult drilling through overburden materials, in low head room situations, and for projects with noise or vibration restrictions. Applicable Soil Conditions: Any soil, rock, or fill conditions including areas with rubble fill, boulders, and karstic conditions. Non-suitable or Difficult Soil Conditions: High slenderness ratio may present buckling problems from loss of lateral support in liquefaction susceptible soils. Low lateral resistance. Offshore applications. | CFA Piles. Use: In groups to transfer heavy loads to suitable geomaterials. Projects with noise and vibration restrictions. Applicable Soil Conditions: Medium to very stiff clays, cemented sands or weak limestone, residual soils, medium dense to dense sands, rock overlain by stiff or cemented deposits. Non-suitable or Difficult Soil Conditions: Very soft soils, loose saturated sands, hard bearing stratum overlain by soft or loose soils, karst conditions, areas with flowing water. Highly variable subsurface conditions. Conditions requiring long piles due to deep scour, liquefiable layers, or penetrating very hard strata or rock, offshore conditions.
sections.applicability: Screening and selection of foundation type based on subsurface conditions, loading, and project constraints.

subsections.title: Shallow Foundations
subsections.body: (p. 49) Spread footings should be considered in any foundation selection and are generally more economical than deep foundations where geomaterial and loading allow: competent soils at shallow depth, a relatively small footing width, an economical depth (e.g., 10 ft) and quality granular fills available (Abu-Hejleh et al. 2014). Spread footings on engineered compacted granular fills and MSE granular fills at bridge abutments have performed well with significant savings. Foundations subject to scour, liquefaction or large settlement, or with large uplift or lateral load demand, are typically not suitable for shallow foundations. See GEC-6 (Kimmerling 2002).
key_points: Spread footings are generally more economical where geomaterial and loading conditions are conducive
Favorable: competent soils at shallow depth, small width, economical depth (e.g., 10 ft), quality granular fill available
Spread footings on compacted granular or MSE fills at abutments: good performance and significant savings
Not suitable: scour, liquefaction, large settlement, large uplift or lateral load demand

subsections.title: Shallow Foundations with Ground Improvement
subsections.body: (p. 49) Ground improvement can make spread footings usable; where strength and service limit states are met the combination should be evaluated economically, as it may cost less than a deep foundation. See FHWA-NHI-06-019/020 Ground Improvement Methods (Elias et al. 2006) and GeoTechTools.org.
key_points: Ground improvement plus spread footings may be more cost effective than deep foundations
Evaluate economically where strength and service limit state requirements are met

subsections.title: Deep Foundations
subsections.body: (pp. 49-51) Deep foundations are generally needed where axial compression, axial tension or lateral load demand cannot be met by the near surface soils, but should not be used indiscriminately: some conditions make a driven pile, drilled shaft, micropile or CFA pile very difficult or costly to install. Ground improvement can also be used with deep foundations to improve lateral resistance in weak surficial soils (Rollins and Brown 2011).
key_points: Needed where near surface soils cannot satisfy axial compression, tension or lateral demand
Not to be used indiscriminately; some conditions make each deep foundation type difficult or costly
Ground improvement can economically improve lateral resistance in weak surficial soils (Rollins and Brown 2011)

subsections.title: Driven Piles
subsections.body: (p. 50) Driven piles are the most commonly used deep foundation for transportation projects, typically installed in groups with an impact hammer. Many pile types and sections resist almost any load demand, and lengths of some types are easily adjusted and spliced in the field for varying subsurface conditions. Pile selection, advantages and disadvantages and the best type for a condition are in Chapter 6.
key_points: Most commonly used deep foundation for transportation projects
Installed in groups with impact hammers; lengths of some types easily adjusted and spliced
Pile type selection guidance in Chapter 6

subsections.title: Drilled Shafts
subsections.body: (p. 50) Drilled shafts are used for large axial compression or lateral load demand. A hole is drilled mechanically or by percussion and filled with concrete, sometimes with a mechanically formed bell; slurry or temporary casing supports unstable sides, and a reinforcing cage is set before concreting. See GEC-10 (Brown et al. 2010) and the AASHTO (2014) design specifications (the printed sentence ends at 'Section' without a number).
key_points: Used for large axial compression or lateral load demand
Drilled hole filled with concrete; bell optional; slurry or temporary casing for unstable holes
Reference GEC-10 (Brown et al. 2010)

subsections.title: Micropiles
subsections.body: (p. 50) Micropiles are used in karst, for underpinning and seismic retrofit, and with difficult drilling. They are small diameter (< 12 in.) reinforced, drilled and grouted elements, often installed by rotating a cased cutting edge or by percussion, cuttings flushed by drilling fluid, reinforcement inserted and sand-cement grout tremied; pressurized two-stage grouting is also used and the casing may be partly or fully withdrawn. See FHWA-NHI-05-039 (Sabatini et al. 2005) and AASHTO (2014) Section 10.9.
key_points: Small diameter (< 12 in.) reinforced, drilled and grouted deep foundation elements
Used in karst, underpinning, seismic retrofit and difficult drilling
Reference FHWA-NHI-05-039 (Sabatini et al. 2005) and AASHTO (2014) Section 10.9

subsections.title: Continuous Flight Auger (CFA) Piles
subsections.body: (p. 51) CFA (or auger cast-in-place, ACIP) piles are installed by turning a continuous-flight hollow-stem auger to depth and pumping grout or concrete under pressure through the stem as it is withdrawn, filling the hole from the bottom up. Vertical reinforcement is pushed into the fresh grout or concrete; an uplift bar can be placed through the hollow stem before grouting; the pile head is cleaned of soil fallen from the auger. See GEC-8 (Brown et al. 2007).
key_points: Hollow-stem auger turned to depth; grout or concrete pumped under pressure as it is withdrawn
Reinforcement pushed into the fresh column; uplift bar may be placed through the stem before grouting
Reference GEC-8 (Brown et al. 2007)

sections.title: Establishment of a Need for a Deep Foundation
sections.summary: Eleven situations requiring deep foundations (Fig 3-1, after Vesic 1977): end bearing to competent stratum (a), friction in deep weak deposit (b), uplift resistance (c), lateral load on single pile (d), battered pile group (e), sign/noise wall (f), scour conditions (g), liquefaction and seismic loading (h), vessel impact fender (i), adjacent future excavation (j), expansive/collapsible soils (k).
sections.body: (pp. 51-53) Vesic (1977) summarized typical situations where piles may be needed, shown in Figure 3-1. The most common case is when upper soil strata are too compressible or too weak to support heavy vertical loads, requiring load transfer to a deeper competent stratum. Deep foundations are also needed to resist inclined, lateral, or uplift loads and overturning moments that shallow footings cannot accommodate. Additional situations include scour conditions, liquefaction and seismic loading, vessel impact protection, future adjacent excavations, and expansive or collapsible soils. Deep foundations transfer load through unsuitable layers to suitable ones, so the designer must define where suitable layers begin. Under HEC-18 (Arneson et al. 2012) all stream bed material in the scour prism is taken as removed and unavailable for bearing or lateral support. Liquefiable soils give less lateral and shaft resistance in an earthquake and can add drag load.
key_points: End bearing piles transfer loads through weak strata to competent bearing layer at depth (Figure 3-1a)
Friction piles transfer loads gradually through shaft resistance when no competent stratum is at reasonable depth (Figure 3-1b)
Deep foundations resist uplift loads through shaft resistance (Figure 3-1c)
Lateral loads resisted by vertical deep foundations in bending (Figure 3-1d) or groups of vertical and battered piles (Figure 3-1e)
Groups of deep foundations support overhead signs and noise walls (Figure 3-1f)
Scour conditions require deep foundations extending below expected scour depth per HEC-18 (Figure 3-1g)
Liquefaction susceptible soils may dictate deep foundations; seismic events add lateral loads and reduce shaft resistance (Figure 3-1h)
Deep foundations used as fender systems for vessel impact protection (Figure 3-1i)
Adjacent future excavations may require deep foundations to avoid future underpinning (Figure 3-1j)
Expansive or collapsible soils require deep foundations to transfer loads to depth unaffected by seasonal moisture movements (Figure 3-1k)
figures: Figure 3-1: Situations in which deep foundations may be needed (modified from Vesic 1977) (p. 53)
sections.applicability: Establishing when deep foundations are required versus shallow foundation alternatives.

sections.title: Economic Aspects of Foundation Selection
sections.summary: Where shallow and deep foundations are both feasible, compare a shallow foundation evaluation (dimensions and depth from bearing resistance, settlement magnitude and rate, detailed cost including cofferdams, dewatering, seals, time, risk and claims) with the feasible deep alternatives; cost generally has a significant role in the final selection.
sections.body: (p. 54) Often both shallow and deep alternatives are technically feasible (feasible spread footing conditions in Abu-Hejleh et al. 2014). The shallow foundation evaluation should include the footing dimensions and depth from bearing resistance, the magnitude and time rate of settlement, and a detailed cost analysis (cofferdams, overall substructure cost, dewatering and seals, construction time and risk, claims potential, other constraints); feasible deep foundation alternatives are compared as well. Cost generally has a significant role in the final selection. The manual deals only with driven piles thereafter.
key_points: Shallow evaluation: footing dimensions and depth from bearing resistance, settlement magnitude and time rate
Detailed cost analysis: cofferdams, substructure cost, dewatering and seals, construction time, risk, claims potential
Feasible deep foundation alternatives are compared as well
Cost analysis generally has a significant role in the final foundation selection
sections.applicability: Economic comparison of technically feasible foundation alternatives using foundation support cost.

sections.title: Foundation Support Cost
sections.summary: Foundation support cost = total foundation cost / factored load supported (tons or kips); for driven piles under axial load it splits into pile, pile cap and construction control method support costs, and includes retention, dewatering, cap size and environmental restrictions (Komurka 2015). Where uplift or lateral load governs, use cost per ton of factored uplift or lateral load.
sections.body: (p. 54) Technically viable foundation systems are compared by their foundation support cost: the total cost of the foundation divided by the factored load it supports, in tons or kips (factored because resistance factors vary by foundation type). For driven piles where axial loading governs, it separates into the pile support cost, the pile cap support cost and the construction control method support cost, and the total includes excavation or retention systems, dewatering, pile caps and cap size and environmental restrictions. Komurka (2015) discusses support cost applications in detail. Where axial tension, lateral or combined loads govern, the cost per ton of factored uplift or lateral load is used. The worked example is Section 3.4.1.1.
key_points: Foundation support cost = total foundation cost / factored load supported ($/ton or $/kip)
Factored loads are used because resistance factors vary by foundation type
Three components for driven piles: pile support cost, pile cap support cost, construction control method support cost
Include excavation or retention systems, dewatering, pile caps and cap size, environmental restrictions
Where tension or lateral load governs, use cost per ton of factored uplift or lateral load
Detailed discussion: Komurka (2015)
sections.applicability: Cost optimization of driven pile foundations using foundation support cost analysis and resistance factor selection.

subsections.title: Cost Optimization Example
subsections.body: (pp. 55-61) A static analysis of an HP 14x117 H-pile by the FHWA method in APILE gives the nominal shaft, toe and total resistance versus depth in a layered profile (Figure 3-2). Candidate terminations: 60 ft in the medium dense sand for 150 kips, 70 ft for 300 kips, 110 ft in the extremely dense sand for 1000 kips, or bedrock near 118 ft for 1700 kips. Pile cost is taken linear with depth (Figure 3-3), except possibly for very long concrete or large steel piles. Dividing cost by nominal resistance gives the nominal resistance pile support cost (Figure 3-4): $39/kip at 60 ft, $19/kip at 70 ft, $9/kip at 110 ft and $5.50/kip at 118 ft (1722 kips), so piles longer than 60 ft are more cost effective. The section's nominal structural resistance is 1720 kips (50 ksi, fully embedded; calculation in Section 8.5.3); the factored structural resistance is 1032 kips with good driving and no shoe, 860 kips with severe driving and a shoe (Figure 3-5). Factored geotechnical resistances use phi_dyn = 0.80 (static load test plus dynamic testing with signal matching on at least two piles and 2 % of production piles), 0.75 (static load test, or signal matching on 100 % of piles), 0.65 (signal matching on two piles and 2 %), 0.50 (wave equation, end of drive) and 0.40 (FHWA modified Gates, end of drive). R_ndr = P_r / phi_dyn and the estimated lengths are in Table 3-3; a drivability check can preclude using the full P_r. For an HP 14x73 (P_r 520 kips in severe driving, static analysis assumed unchanged) the length is 104 ft with phi_dyn 0.80 against 116 ft with 0.40. For uplift (Figures 3-6, 3-7) the support cost has plateaus of $90-100/kip above 60 ft and $15-25/kip below 70 ft, and phi_up = 0.60 (static load test), 0.50 (dynamic test with signal matching), 0.25 in clay and 0.35 in sand (alpha-method and Nordlund).

Support cost ($/kip) = pile cost / nominal resistance: $39 at 60 ft, $19 at 70 ft, $9 at 110 ft, $5.50 at 118 ft (1722 kips)

Uplift support cost plateaus: $90-100/kip above 60 ft, $15-25/kip below 70 ft

sections.title: Other Considerations
sections.summary: Non-economic factors in foundation selection: constructability and drivability, pile driving noise, ground vibrations, condition surveys and vibration monitoring of adjacent facilities, and durability. Environmental restrictions on vibrations, noise, and work hours can significantly increase foundation costs.
sections.body: (pp. 61-62) Beyond technical feasibility and economics, several additional factors must be evaluated when selecting a driven pile foundation. These include constructability, pile driving noise, pile driving induced vibrations, condition surveys and vibration monitoring of adjacent facilities, and durability considerations. Environmental restrictions on vibrations, noise, and work hours can significantly increase foundation costs and should be factored into the selection process.
key_points: Constructability, noise, vibrations, effects on nearby structures, durability, and long-term maintenance must be evaluated
Environmental restrictions on vibrations, noise, work hours, and marine life will increase costs
Multiple driven pile alternatives may be technically feasible; other considerations guide final selection
sections.applicability: Non-economic factors influencing driven pile foundation selection.

sections.title: Constructability
sections.summary: Drivability must be verified: the pile must reach the specified minimum penetration depth. Design must consider hard layers requiring predrilling or jetting, densification within cofferdams, heave from displacement piles in cohesive soils, and constraints on headroom, workspace, and construction access.
sections.body: (p. 62) Constructability should be assessed during design with construction considerations factored into pile selection and final design. Drivability is a key component: the chosen pile section must be capable of being installed to the specified minimum penetration depth. The design and drivability assessment should consider hard layers requiring predrilling or jetting, potential densification effects in cofferdams or from driving large pile groups, heave effects on adjacent structures from displacement piles in cohesive deposits, and limitations on head room, work space, and construction access.
key_points: Drivability must be evaluated to ensure pile can be installed to required penetration depth
Hard layers that must be penetrated may require predrilling or jetting
Potential densification of soils within cofferdams or from driving large pile groups must be considered
Soil heave from displacement piles in cohesive deposits can affect adjacent structures and utilities
Head room, work space, and construction access limitations increase driven pile foundation costs
Environmental restrictions on vibrations, noise, work hours, marine mammals, and fish increase costs
sections.applicability: Constructability assessment during design phase for driven pile foundations.

sections.title: Consideration of Pile Driving Noise
sections.summary: Impact pile driving noise typically ranges from 80–135 dBa. Noise suppression devices available for some diesel/hydraulic hammers can reduce levels by ~10 dBa. Costs of noise restrictions (work hour limits, equipment type, suppression devices) must be included in foundation cost estimates.
sections.body: (pp. 62-63) Noise from impact pile driving typically ranges from 80 to 135 dBa depending on hammer and pile type. If local ordinances dictate allowable noise levels at or below typical driving levels, some equipment may not comply. A few diesel and hydraulic hammer manufacturers offer optional noise suppression devices that may reduce noise by about 10 dBa. In noise sensitive areas, the designer should review ordinances and assess impacts on contractor equipment selection and productivity. Costs associated with work hour limits, equipment type restrictions, and noise suppression equipment should be included in the foundation selection process.
key_points: Impact pile driving noise typically ranges from 80 to 135 dBa
Local noise ordinances may restrict driving equipment that exceeds allowable levels
Noise suppression devices on some diesel and hydraulic hammers can reduce noise by about 10 dBa
Independently manufactured noise suppression devices are also available
Costs of noise restrictions (work hour limits, equipment type, suppression devices) should be included in foundation cost estimates
Additional noise suppression information is presented in Chapter 15
sections.applicability: Evaluation of pile driving noise impacts and mitigation for noise-sensitive project locations.

sections.title: Pile Driving Induced Vibrations
sections.summary: Damage threshold 0.5–4 in/sec peak particle velocity (Wiss 1981). Settlement can occur at PPV as low as 0.1–0.2 in/sec in loose sands. Bay (2003) gives PPV vs. distance for Class II (n=1.5) and Class III (n=1.1) soils by hammer energy (Fig 3-8). Massarsch & Fellenius (2014) settlement in inverted 2V:1H zone: S_max = alpha*(D+6b), S_avg = alpha*(D+3b)/3 (Eqs 3-1, 3-2).
sections.body: (pp. 63-68) Ground vibrations from impact or vibratory pile driving are always induced into surrounding soils. Vibration levels depend on soil type, pile type and section, hammer type, penetration resistance, pile toe depth, and distance from the pile. Damage to nearby structures can result from vibration-induced soil densification and settlement, or from direct vibration effects on the structure. Wiss (1981) recommended safe ground vibration levels of 0.5 to 4 inches per second peak particle velocity. Bay (2003) summarized relationships between peak particle velocity and distance from the pile as a function of rated hammer energy for Class II and Class III soils (Figure 3-8). Massarsch and Fellenius (2014) describe vibration-induced settlement using Equations 3-1 and 3-2 within an inverted 2(V):1(H) triangular zone around the pile. Lacy and Gould (1985) found settlements at ground surface peak particle velocities as low as 0.1 to 0.2 in/sec, in late Pleistocene sands with uniformity coefficients up to 4 or 5 and relative densities up to 50 or 55 %. Under NFPA 495 (2013) the limit is frequency dependent: 1 in/sec at 30 Hz is within the limits, at 10 Hz above them. Table 3-4 gives alpha from 0.02 (very loose, low vibration) to 0.04 (very loose, high) down to 0.00 (dense or very dense, low). The Pile Driving Contractors Association (2015) database holds 23 case histories and over 1800 measurements, for general guidance only.
key_points: Vibrations depend on soil type, pile type/section, hammer, penetration resistance, toe depth, and distance from pile
Damage from two mechanisms: vibration-induced soil densification/settlement and direct vibration effects on structures
Significant settlements can occur at peak particle velocities as low as 0.1-0.2 in/sec in loose sands
Typically recommended 'safe' levels 0.5-4 in/sec peak particle velocity (Wiss 1981); NFPA 495 limits are frequency-dependent
Bay (2003): Class II soils (SPT-N 5-15, n=1.5) and Class III soils (SPT-N 15-50, n=1.1) vibration charts
Pile impedance EA/C affects vibration: low impedance piles transmit more energy to soil along shaft
Massarsch and Fellenius (2014): settlement in inverted 2V:1H triangular zone, max settlement S_max = alpha*(D+6b), average settlement S_avg = alpha*(D+3b)/3
Mitigation techniques include predrilling, jetting, cutoff trenches, different pile type, or different hammer
Vibration specification should include frequency-dependent maximum peak particle velocity limits and predriving survey
Vibration damage unlikely at distances >50 ft for piles <=50 ft long, or >1 pile length for piles >50 ft long

sections.title: Condition Surveys and Vibration Monitoring of Adjacent Facilities
sections.summary: Pre-construction condition surveys (photos, video, crack monitors) document existing conditions as a baseline for damage claims; a post-construction survey records any change. Routine survey distance: 200 ft from pile driving, extended to as much as 500 ft for older structures, structures in poor condition, or vibration-sensitive equipment. Use film rather than digital photography if damage claims may arise. Vibration monitoring by experienced personnel where structures, facilities or utilities lie in the affected zone.
sections.body: (p. 68) Pre-construction condition surveys and vibration monitoring programs are warranted on projects in populated urban areas. Prior to construction, the internal and external condition of potentially affected structures should be documented using photos and videos, including existing cracks with crack monitors installed. This provides a baseline for comparison against any future damage claims. Post-construction surveys should document any changes. Condition surveys should use film rather than digital photography if damage claims may arise. Survey distances for routine cases should extend 200 feet from pile driving, extended to 500 feet for older structures, structures in poor condition, or vibration-sensitive equipment.
key_points: Pre-construction condition surveys document existing conditions as baseline for damage claims
Document internal and external condition using photos, videos, and crack monitors
Post-construction survey should document any changes to existing structures
Use film rather than digital photography for potential damage claim evidence
Advance notification to neighbors, pre-construction surveys, and vibration monitoring promote good neighbor policy and reduce claims
Routine survey distance: 200 feet from pile driving operation
Extended survey distance (up to 500 feet) for older structures, poor condition structures, or vibration-sensitive equipment
Vibration monitoring by experienced personnel should be performed when structures, facilities, or utilities are within the potentially affected zone
sections.applicability: Pre-construction and post-construction documentation for pile driving projects near existing structures.

sections.title: Durability Considerations
sections.summary: AASHTO mandates 75-year design life for ordinary bridges, 100 years for complex major bridges. Steel pile corrosion (case: Leo Frigo Bridge 2013, 32-yr H-piles in fly ash fill). Concrete piles: chloride/sulfate attack, abrasion. Timber piles: creosote-treated last 40-70 years depending on channel exposure. The text points to Section 6.13 for steel pile protection; the aggressive-environment guidance is Section 6.12.
sections.body: (pp. 68-72) The durability of a pile foundation is defined by how long it performs satisfactorily without unforeseen high maintenance costs relative to the expected service life. AASHTO mandates a 75-year design life for new ordinary bridges, with 100 years for complex major bridges. In general, driven piles have proved very durable in most environments, but aggressive environments can cause significant deterioration. Steel pile corrosion was the cause of the 2013 Leo Frigo Bridge (I-43) settlement in Green Bay, WI, where 32-year-old H-piles experienced severe corrosion from porous industrial fly ash fill, sulfates, and chlorides. Concrete piles can deteriorate from chloride intrusion, reinforcement corrosion, tidal/splash zone abrasion, and sulfate attack. Timber piles experience mechanical damage, abrasion, fire damage, and weathering; creosote-treated timber piles away from stream channels last 60-70 years while those in channels have a 40-50 year life expectancy.
key_points: AASHTO mandates 75-year design life for ordinary bridges; 100 years for complex major bridges
Driven piles are generally very durable but aggressive environments can cause rapid deterioration
Steel pile corrosion case: Leo Frigo Bridge (2013), Green Bay, WI - 32-year-old H-piles in porous fly ash fill with sulfates and chlorides caused 2-foot pier settlement
Corrosion study of 34-year-old H-piles (Girard Avenue Bridge, Philadelphia) found 12% section loss; site-specific rate of 0.0015 in/year was less than published rates
Concrete pile deterioration: chloride intrusion, reinforcement/prestressing strand corrosion, tidal/splash zone abrasion, sulfate attack
Some prestressed concrete piles in coastal Georgia had severe corrosion damage in less than 25 years of service
Multiple deterioration mechanisms can combine: chloride corrosion + sulfate attack + biological boring (Holland et al. 2014)
High performance concrete mixes being studied to improve concrete pile durability in aggressive environments
Timber pile durability issues: mechanical damage, abrasion/debris, fire damage, weathering; creosote-treated piles last 60-70 years (away from channel) or 40-50 years (in channel)
Section 6.13 provides details on steel pile protection measures and durability design

sections.title: Unanticipated Occurrences
sections.summary: Outside influences can damage existing foundations. Section 3.6.1: a roughly 50,000 ton fill stockpile beside four I-495 piers in Delaware (summer 2014, printed '2104') moved the soil laterally, deformed H-piles, cracked caps and tilted 50 ft columns almost 2 ft. Section 3.6.2: driving H-piles to widen I-65 over Wildcat Creek (2015) released artesian pressure and sand beneath the adjacent spread footing pier, which settled up to 10 in. and rotated 7 in.
sections.body: (pp. 72-74) The long term performance of a foundation is generally assessed by total and differential settlement within and between substructure locations. Outside influences can affect it unexpectedly: a fill stockpile beside existing piers (Section 3.6.1) or a new pile foundation built beside an existing one (Section 3.6.2).
key_points: Foundation long-term performance assessed by total and differential settlement
Unanticipated outside influences can compromise existing foundation performance
Two cases: a fill stockpile beside piers (3.6.1) and adjacent new pile construction (3.6.2)
sections.applicability: Awareness of how external activities and unanticipated events can damage existing driven pile foundations.

subsections.title: Fill Stockpile
subsections.body: (pp. 73-74) In the summer of 2014 (printed '2104') part of the 40 year old elevated I-495 near Wilmington, Delaware tilted over a short period; the tops of some 50 ft columns were almost 2 ft out of alignment (Figure 3-14). A roughly 50,000 ton fill stockpile near four piers had moved the soil laterally beneath the bridge, deformed the supporting H-piles and cracked the pile caps (Figure 3-15). The structure had performed as expected until the stockpile.
key_points: I-495 near Wilmington, Delaware, summer 2014 (printed '2104'): columns 50 ft tall nearly 2 ft out of alignment
A roughly 50,000 ton fill stockpile caused lateral soil movement, deformed H-piles and cracked pile caps
Four piers tilted; the structure had performed as expected until the stockpile
figures: Figure 3-14: Tilting columns adjacent to stockpile (courtesy DelDOT) (p. 73)
Figure 3-15: Cracked pile cap from lateral soil movements (courtesy DelDOT) (p. 74)

subsections.title: Adjacent Construction
subsections.body: (p. 74) In 2015 the five span I-65 bridge over Wildcat Creek was widened from two to three lanes; for scour the new work was on driven H-piles rather than spread footings. Shortly after production driving, the adjacent pier on spread footings settled as much as 10 in. and rotated 7 in. (ENR 2015) and the bridge was closed to stabilize it. The movements were attributed to the release of artesian pressures and sand beneath the spread footing pier.
key_points: I-65 over Wildcat Creek, 2015: widening on driven H-piles (for scour) beside a pier on spread footings
The existing pier settled up to 10 in. and rotated 7 in.; the bridge was closed to stabilize it
Attributed to release of artesian pressures and sand beneath the spread footing pier
